💣❌ 40 million reasons why Pakistan refrains from fighting the Houthis
Pakistan has the second-largest Shia community in the world — 40 million people, about 20% of the population.
In 2026, after the death of Iranian leader Ali Khamenei, mass Shia protests erupted in Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad. In Karachi alone, at least 9 people were killed in clashes near the American consulate.
The Houthis are a Shia movement of the Zaidi branch. This confessional proximity matters for Islamabad — it is a real internal security factor. Direct participation in the anti-Houthi campaign risks triggering sectarian violence at home.
👉 Still, the Shia factor is not the only reason for Pakistan's restraint. The economy depends on energy supplies through the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz. Strategically, Pakistan does not want to choose between Saudi Arabia and Iran, which backs the Houthis. Islamabad even asked Tehran to influence the Houthis diplomatically. Joining the anti-Houthi campaign would disrupt this fragile balance.
Despite the Mecca Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan has so far avoided any direct military involvement in Yemen. Its Foreign Ministry has stated that "no military operations are being discussed" and that the pact "is purely defensive in nature."

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇵🇰🗣 Pakistan will go "to any extent" to defend Saudi Arabia — but what does that mean in practice?
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry stated that Pakistan will go "to any extent" to defend Saudi Arabia. According to him, Islamabad's commitment to the Kingdom's security is "unconditional" and extends to the protection of Mecca and Madinah. "We are present there to protect the Two Holy Mosques. There should be no doubt on that," he emphasized.
Recall that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia are bound by a mutual defense pact — the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) — as well as the recently formed trilateral Mecca Defense Alliance involving Turkey. Formally, this means an attack on one member of the alliance is an attack on all.
However, since the start of a series of heavy Houthi strikes on Saudi territory, Pakistani officials have given contradictory signals.
1️⃣ General Chaudhry (September 17) pledged absolute physical intervention but refused to clarify whether Riyadh had requested troops or weapons.
2️⃣ Pakistan's Foreign Office (September 17) on the same day spoke only of commitment to the pact "in intent and spirit," toning down the military's belligerent rhetoric.
3️⃣ Defense Minister Khawaja Asif (September 9) stated that an attack on Saudi Arabia would automatically trigger collective defense. But within days, diplomatic sources and Turkish officials clarified: no combat forces are being deployed, and the pact's operational details remain unformulated.
4️⃣ Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (September 8) condemned the "cowardly" attacks and reaffirmed "unwavering" solidarity — but remained silent on the conflict's structural causes.
According to media reports, Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir called Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to ask him to influence the Houthis. Iran confirmed the call took place, but not its details.
In short: Pakistan is balancing between loud promises to its ally and an unwillingness to be dragged into a hot war.
